We further propose CSWEval, a theory-informed framework with two complementary levels: event-level evaluation of Licensing, Contextual Appropriateness, and Functional Gain, and whole-text evaluation of task-specific quality---overall literary and narrative quality in Focused Narrative and quality emphasizing multilingual organization in Extended Narrative. Evaluating twelve LLMs, we find that models exhibit meaningful but uneven code-switching competence across narrative contexts. Model differences are particularly pronounced in multilingual literary integration, while multilingual-focused dimensions show stronger difficulty effects overall than the general narrative dimensions; narratively salient switches are associated with stronger contextual and functional realization; and event-level CS quality is moderately associated with whole-text performance.
2610.20272.COMMENT: No direct match to any specific criterion. The paper introduces a benchmark and evaluation framework for context-sensitive code-switching in creative writing by LLMs. While it involves evaluation, it is task-specific and does not fundamentally rethink open-ended text generation evaluation or address subjectivity or adversarial evaluation paradigms. It is more about multilingual generation competence than general evaluation paradigms or generative modeling advances.

2610.17840.title: Learning Adaptive Deliberation Control for Reliable Recognition with Multi-Agent Language Models
2610.17840.abstract: arXiv:2610.17840v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Multi-agent deliberation can improve recognition by criticizing and revising candidate answers, but fixed controls cannot respond to changes in disagreement or reasoning quality. We present an adaptive multi-agent controller (ADMA) that learns continuous policies for proposal, challenge, arbitration, and coordination while keeping the task model frozen. Shared trace features describe quality, agreement, and progress, while role-specific features support decentralized control during inference. One controller trained on legal and financial reasoning is transferred without policy updates to four textual and multimodal benchmarks and two successive task-model versions. With Qwen3.5 held fixed, ADMA-Full improves accuracy by 6.2-14.2 percentage points over Direct and by 2.8-3.0 points over ADMA-Fixed. Paired bootstrap ranges for the Full-Fixed comparison are positive on three tasks. Outcome decompositions show that recoveries exceed introduced errors, while process assessment records fewer false-consensus events and more supported correct outcomes. Transfer to Qwen3.6 remains task dependent, which bounds the generality of the learned policy. Median token and latency ratios are 14.3-18.7 and 7.8-16.5 relative to Direct. These results show that adaptive deliberation can improve fixed-model recognition when its task-dependent gains justify the additional computation.
2610.17840.COMMENT: Related to multi-agent deliberation and adaptive control for recognition tasks, but does not match any specific criterion about RLHF, contamination, diffusion LMs, or evaluation paradigms.

2610.14190.title: Cross-Modal Latent Influence: Patch-Level Training Sample Attribution for Vision-Language Models
2610.14190.abstract: arXiv:2610.14190v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Explaining a vision--language model (VLM) prediction requires tracing training-example influence to the multimodal evidence that mediates it, yet existing attribution methods largely operate only at the sample level. Recent latent-mediated influence methods provide feature-level attribution in language models, but lack the multimodal and spatial structure needed to ground influence in VLMs. We introduce MOSAIC (Multimodal Orthogonalized Sparse Autoencoders for Influence Characterization). It learns a shared sparse image--text latent space whose concepts are 1) sparse within each modality, 2) supported on contiguous image regions, 3) aligned to the phrases that describe them, and 4) approximately decorrelated. It then applies EK-FAC to decompose training-example influence through these concepts and localize their contributions to specific text phrases and image regions. We evaluate MOSAIC on Qwen and Gemma across captioning, chest X-ray understanding, and visual question answering. The learned features are more localized and coherent without degrading task behavior, and ablating influence-ranked latents changes model outputs more than ablating latents ranked by activation or frequency. We find that visual evidence can substantially reorganize training-data attribution while preserving more of the shared latent structure. MOSAIC thus connects where model behavior comes from with what multimodal evidence carries that influence.
2610.14190.COMMENT: No direct match to any specific criterion. Although it involves sparse autoencoders, it is for influence attribution in vision-language models, not sparse autoencoders for interpretability of neural networks (criterion 7). Not about RLHF, contamination, diffusion LMs, or evaluation paradigms.

2610.19427.title: How Do LLMs Understand Legal Philosophy? Diagnosing Legal-Philosophical Reasoning in LLMs
2610.19427.abstract: arXiv:2610.19427v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Legal reasoning is a fundamental capability for large language models (LLMs) to complete legal AI tasks such as legal judgment prediction. In legal practice, this reasoning is shaped by legal philosophy: a judge's view of the nature and sources of law guides how legal materials are interpreted and applied, so judges working from the same statutes and precedents can reach different judgments. Existing research has largely overlooked whether LLMs can understand legal philosophy and apply it in legal reasoning, an ability we call \textit{legal-philosophical reasoning}. To fill this gap, we introduce LePhilBench, a benchmark for evaluating the legal-philosophical reasoning of LLMs that comprises two benchmarking tasks and a dataset. The two tasks evaluate how well LLMs understand legal philosophy and how well they apply it in legal reasoning, respectively. The dataset is manually and meticulously constructed. Its test set contains 220 U.S. Supreme Court opinions. A law professor designed fourteen annotation questions on legal philosophy, and three law-trained annotators with formal training in jurisprudence answered all fourteen questions for every opinion, yielding 9,240 legal-philosophical labels. LePhilBench takes the first step toward exploring legal-philosophical reasoning in LLMs.
2610.19427.COMMENT: No direct match to any specific criterion. The paper focuses on legal-philosophical reasoning in LLMs, which is an application domain and evaluation of reasoning ability but not a new paradigm for open-ended evaluation or reasoning mechanisms.

2610.19848.title: OpenTWBench (Open Taiwan Benchmark): Taiwan-Domain Knowledge Evaluation for Large Language Models, and How the Measurement Apparatus Shapes the Score
2610.19848.abstract: arXiv:2610.19848v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: We present OpenTWBench, an open evaluation suite for Taiwan-domain knowledge in large language models, built around two benchmarks. tw-exam-bench contains 255,854 four-option questions across 148 academic subjects, from fifteen years of Taiwan's national examinations published as open data by the Ministry of Examination; answer keys agree across 31,312 duplicated question groups at 99.91%, with all 27 disagreements accounted for. A reviewed second pass withdrew 2,180 items whose stems depend on a figure the text does not carry; all scores use the remaining 253,674. tw-formosa-bench contains 1,696 difficulty-curated questions about everyday and contemporary Taiwan - the Taiwan that licensing examinations never ask about - generated from a community-curated corpus under a discipline in which no model writes a ground truth, and curated against a frozen seven-model pool so that the pool scored at the passing margin (46.9-74.6%, median ~54%); a leave-one-out experiment shows the selection preserves model ranking (near-zero bias). Within six weeks the frontier had cleared that band: of 108 models now on the public board, 22 score above its ceiling, the best 91.6%.   We also document how much of a score comes from the apparatus rather than the model. On identical questions, switching answer extraction from pattern matching to an explicit \boxed{} answer moves accuracy from 20.8% to 93.9%; a single placeholder character in a system prompt moved one model from last (58.2%) to first (83.9%) on the same benchmark; doubling the thinking budget from 8k to 16k tokens bought 0.2% while shuffling which questions failed; and a three-judge validation panel proved to be one judge in disguise, two members approving 92-99% of everything shown. We release all datasets, per-item difficulty data, curation manifests and a leaderboard at https://opentwbench.ai
2610.19848.COMMENT: This paper is primarily about benchmarking and evaluation of LLMs on Taiwan-domain knowledge, with detailed analysis of evaluation apparatus effects. It does not fundamentally rethink open-ended text generation evaluation (criterion 4), nor does it propose new methods for instruction-following or RLHF (criterion 1). It is closest to criterion 5 (real-world usage and safety properties) but only tangentially, as it focuses on domain-specific benchmarks rather than broad usage or safety surveys.

2610.17869.title: ECMR: Evidence-Aware Deliberation Control for Multi-Agent LLM Reasoning
2610.17869.abstract: arXiv:2610.17869v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Multi-agent Large Language Model (LLM) systems typically commit to a deliberation protocol before inference. A fixed protocol cannot allocate computation differently to resolved and unresolved instances, and it may mistake repeated support for independent confirmation. We study this failure as semantic false consensus: a confident group answer supported by narrow, duplicated, or correlated rationales. We introduce ECMR, an evidence-aware controller over frozen role-conditioned LLMs. At each step, ECMR summarizes answer concentration, support diversity and independence, contradictions, role behavior, verification history, and remaining budget, then selects whether to propose, challenge, verify, arbitrate, diversify, correct a role, or stop. We formulate this decision as finite-horizon budgeted control and derive sufficient conditions under which state conditioning, risk-triggered verification, and role correction improve cost-adjusted utility. Across a declared held-out evaluation of 9,000 records from MedQA, CaseHOLD, and FinQA, ECMR-Full increases pooled accuracy from 62.1% to 84.9%, reduces false-consensus rate from 40.7% to 17.0%, and raises evidence-support rate from 58.0% to 88.7%. State shuffling loses 11.7 accuracy points with only 0.7 fewer rounds, while harder traces shift from early stopping toward arbitration. ECMR-Full uses the largest token budget, yielding the strongest absolute reliability rather than uniformly superior token efficiency.
2610.17869.COMMENT: No direct match to specific criteria. The paper focuses on multi-agent LLM reasoning control and deliberation protocols, which relates to reasoning and multi-agent systems but does not specifically address instruction-following fine-tuning, contamination, diffusion LMs, or evaluation paradigms as per criteria.

2610.19344.title: Target-Token Asymmetry Can Masquerade As Depth Specialization
2610.19344.abstract: arXiv:2610.19344v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Layer-ablation studies often perturb early or late layers of a language model, compare the damage to prediction on two corpora, and read a larger early-layer effect on one corpus as early-layer specialization for its task. Such a comparison averages over the tokens that each corpus asks the model to predict, and these target tokens differ: math solutions, for example, ask for far more whitespace and numbers than encyclopedia prose. We show that this difference can create the appearance of depth specialization. We split a cross-corpus early--late damage interaction by target-token type and recompute it under a target mixture shared by both corpora. Between GSM8K and Wikitext, a positive interaction replicates across five model instances. In the three fully decomposed models, only whitespace has a positive interaction. Removing whitespace reverses the pooled effect in all three, and matching the full target mixture reverses it in two. The diagnosis holds under position matching, adversarial reassignment of token types, and a continuous readout. The risk can also be anticipated from the tokenizer alone. A screen computed before any model runs places every held-out pair it scored in the region its label predicts, and on the pairs it rates at high or medium risk, removing whitespace reverses every positive pooled estimate. A smaller content-word effect one token ahead follows the share of content targets that the unablated model already predicts. A cross-corpus depth effect therefore supports an interpretation of task specialization only after the target-token mixture is reported, the effect is decomposed by token type, and a mixture-matched summary keeps its sign.
2610.19344.COMMENT: Related to analysis of layer specialization and token-type effects in language models, but does not match any specific criterion about instruction-following, contamination, diffusion, or interpretability. Mostly an empirical analysis of token effects on depth specialization, not a new method or evaluation paradigm.

2610.18067.title: WorkRover: Scaling Long-Horizon Cowork Agent Training Via Recursive Environment Evolution
2610.18067.abstract: arXiv:2610.18067v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Scaling interactive environments is important for training long-horizon agents through reinforcement learning. These environments often require further testing and refinement after initial generation, and correcting defects in a task may also require updating its work context and verifier. However, existing construction pipelines offer limited support for such iterative refinement while keeping these components aligned. We introduce WorkRover, a framework for training long-horizon cowork agents through recursive environment evolution. Its harness-driven synthesis enables construction agents to jointly build and validate semantically aligned work contexts, executable tasks, and evidence-grounded verifiers, adapting their actions to workspace state and execution feedback rather than following a fixed construction workflow. To support environment evolution, we introduce Factorial Compatibility Replay (FCR), which uses rollout feedback to evaluate combinations of component revisions through dependency-closed replay and selects the smallest validated repair among tested candidates while preserving task requirements and evaluation constraints. To provide finer-grained training signals, we propose Verifier-to-Turn Credit Assignment (VTCA), which augments trajectory-level GRPO advantages with signals from deterministic workspace-progress checks and assigns a bounded share of positive-progress credit to prerequisite turns using recorded tool-output and artifact dependencies. Using WorkRover, we post-train Qwen3.5-35B-A3B to obtain WorkRover-35B-A3B and evaluate it on several cowork-agent benchmarks. Its reported scores exceed those of Qwen3.5-35B-A3B by 26.27 percentage points on JobBench, 29.32 percentage points on OfficeQA Pro, and 413.25 Elo points on GDPval v2. These results suggest that WorkRover offers a promising foundation for scalable training of long-horizon cowork agents.
2610.18067.COMMENT: No direct match to any specific criterion. The paper focuses on training long-horizon cowork agents via recursive environment evolution and reinforcement learning techniques, but does not explicitly discuss RLHF, instruction-following fine-tuning, test set contamination, diffusion LMs, or evaluation paradigms.

2610.17271.title: Reasoning for Propaganda Detection via Label-Guided CoT Optimisation
2610.17271.abstract: arXiv:2610.17271v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Propaganda detection systems usually operate as black boxes, lacking explanations. To address this, we hypothesise that persuasive techniques contain definitional characteristics with respect to their social-political setting. We introduce ReCoT, a reasoning-conditioned detection framework that captures definitional cues of persuasive techniques via population-level refinement and performance-guided resampling, without requiring additional explanation annotations. On INDI-PROPspan, ReCoT achieves a macro F1_LCS of 0.364, surpassing baselines and reaching 88% of the SFT upper bound on Avg F1_LCS. Similarly, on PTC, ReCoT reaches 85% of the SFT upper bound on Avg F1_LCS, closing much of this gap while remaining interpretable. Importantly, the analysis of the reasoning pool's convergence and update pattern for ReCoT shows effective refinement of reasoning CoTs.
2610.17271.COMMENT: No specific criteria matched. Although it involves reasoning and chain-of-thought, it is applied to propaganda detection and does not fundamentally rethink open-ended evaluation or reasoning transparency.

2610.15235.title: MoMaTune: Model, Match, Then Tune Language Models for Numerical Records
2610.15235.abstract: arXiv:2610.15235v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Despite remarkable progress in language understanding and generation, decoder language models continue to exhibit striking failures on numerical data. Numerical examples are typically serialized as text by concatenating feature names with their values (e.g., fat:3.4), while conventional task adaptation applies loss only to the downstream prediction target. This leaves two structures weakly supervised: within-value sensitivity, where digit position determines numerical magnitude, because token cross-entropy contains no explicit numerical metric; and across-field structure, where measurements in the same record are statistically dependent, because target-only tuning provides no direct loss on the measurements or their dependencies. We introduce MoMaTune (Model, Match, then Tune), a two-stage post-training strategy organized around these supervision gaps. Stage 1 applies Model, ordinary next-token prediction densely over label-free serialized records, and optionally adds Match, a same-record consistency objective that aligns representations of different partial views of the same example. Stage 2 applies Tune, supervised fine-tuning for downstream target prediction. We evaluate MoMaTune on 169,285 records from eight public datasets, with 339 of 340 input fields numerical. At 1.5B parameters, Model raises the eight-dataset masked-value imputation aggregate from 0.106 to 0.401, while the three-dataset correct-context gain rises from 0.058 to 0.167. On diagnostics, Model also increases sensitivity to numerically consequential digit changes, while Match improves robustness to informative partial views. Adding Tune yields higher target-supervised embedding aggregates for each tested Stage-1 parent, and the two-stage recipes obtain higher aggregate scores than Tune alone. The same pattern is observed at 4B, 9.6B, and 27B parameters when model embeddings are used for downstream prediction.
2610.15235.COMMENT: No direct match to any specific criterion. The paper proposes a two-stage fine-tuning strategy for numerical data in language models, focusing on improving numerical understanding and robustness, but does not address RLHF, instruction-following fine-tuning, test contamination, diffusion LMs, or other listed criteria.

2610.19349.title: Where to Start, How to Move: Analyzing Curricula under GRPO for Long-Horizon LLM Agents
2610.19349.abstract: arXiv:2610.19349v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) provides no reward-relative learning signal when all rollouts receive identical rewards. In long-horizon tasks that require multiple interactions, rewards are given only upon successful task completion, making all-fail groups common early in training and limiting opportunities to practice later steps. Guide Assisted GRPO replays a successful reference prefix before the learner continues. We study how initial positions, handoff units, and movement rules affect unassisted task completion. Across three model sizes on BFCL, starting near completion is more effective under a fixed turn-level threshold rule. Finer handoffs alone do not consistently help, but outcome-informed tool-call selection outperforms GRPO on trained and untrained task categories. Guided starts also improve AppWorld success on both evaluation splits. These findings highlight where learning starts and how starting positions move as key curriculum choices.
2610.19349.COMMENT: This paper studies curriculum design for long-horizon LLM agents but does not focus on RLHF, instruction-following fine-tuning, or any of the specific criteria related to instruction tuning or contamination. It is more about reinforcement learning curriculum strategies.

2610.15150.title: Harmony Harness: Multi-Objective Self-Evolution of Agent Harnesses
2610.15150.abstract: arXiv:2610.15150v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Recent work on self-evolving LLM agents treats the agent harness as an optimization target that can be iteratively improved through execution feedback. Existing approaches, however, largely optimize a single objective and evolve the harness as a monolithic artifact, limiting their ability to handle competing goals and to separate transferable design from environment-specific adaptation. We introduce Harmony Harness, a framework for multi-objective, compositional harness evolution. Harmony Harness formulates harness evolution as a multi-objective optimization problem and uses decomposition-based evolutionary search to maintain solutions across different regions of the Pareto frontier, avoiding reliance on a hand-designed structural diversity metric for repository-scale harnesses. In parallel, we introduce factorized evolution operators that separately refine general-purpose harness mechanisms and benchmark-specific adaptations, together with a dynamic composition workflow that integrates them at inference time. Across SecRepoBench and BaxBench, Harmony Harness consistently outperforms strong harness-evolution baselines, with gains exceeding 10% on both benchmarks. Our results show that explicitly modeling both objective trade-offs and harness structure yields substantially stronger and more transferable agent evolution than existing single-objective, monolithic approaches.
2610.15150.COMMENT: This paper proposes a multi-objective evolutionary framework for improving agent harnesses, which relates to improving agent behavior but does not specifically address RLHF, instruction-following fine-tuning, or instruction-tuning datasets. No direct match to criteria 1 or others.

2610.15204.title: SocraticRepair: Planning-Guided Socratic Tutoring for Program Debugging and Misconception Repair
2610.15204.abstract: arXiv:2610.15204v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Large language models are increasingly used in computer science education. However, the teaching abilities of even the most powerful LLMs are limited: they tend to reveal the solution prematurely and may lose focus on the learner's current debugging objective. To address this, we introduce SocraticRepair, a planning-guided Socratic tutoring framework for program debugging and miscon- ception repair that adapts prior planning-guided tutoring work (Li et al., 2026b). The framework is instantiated in the Python programming domain by fine-tuning Qwen2.5-Coder-7B-Instruct on synthetic multi-turn tutoring dialogues constructed from four preprocessed programming datasets. The system is evaluated using a predefined set of independent metrics and benchmarked against a general-purpose LLM. The experiments show that SocraticRepair achieves higher scores on stepwise scaffolding and question quality while also substantially reducing premature solution disclosure. The results also identify reliable pedagogical plan generation as an important remaining challenge.
2610.15204.COMMENT: No direct match to any specific criterion. The paper focuses on fine-tuning an LLM for Socratic tutoring in program debugging, which is an application of instruction-following but does not propose new methodological improvements to RLHF or instruction-following methods themselves (criterion 1).

2610.14428.title: Frustratingly Easy Agentic RAG via Portable Skills: A Case Study in Customer Support
2610.14428.abstract: arXiv:2610.14428v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Enterprise workflow automation typically requires retrieving a complete and accurate set of relevant information from large operational document corpora (SOPs, policy documents) given a specific scenario or request. In customer support (CS), for example, human specialists must determine the correct sequence of resolution steps for each case, a task that demands precise grounding in policy documentation. Meeting this bar in production typically requires complex document chunking, indexing, and retrieval pipelines, often layered with learned re-rankers, query rewriters, and bespoke agentic RAG infrastructure.   We report a deployment case study of a simpler alternative: a portable skill consisting of a natural-language instruction, lightweight tools (a retrieval API, format-checking scripts), and a corpus enriched with an LLM-generated navigation layer, which is a structured "Wikipedia-style" index over the underlying documents. This agentic RAG approach is straightforward to implement (1-2 engineer days), portable across capable agentic harnesses (e.g., Claude Code), and performs strongly on the challenging task of CS resolution workflow generation, achieving 99.2% procedural equivalence to human-approved ground truth and 83.3% evidence sufficiency. It is also roughly an order of magnitude slower per case than our deployed production assistant (~90 s vs. ~8-9 s), so we claim no latency advantage. Our claim is scoped to that setting: a mature, well-curated corpus, a latency-tolerant workflow, and human review of every case. There, the skill did the work of a complex RAG stack, and maintenance became a matter of editing text and data rather than retraining models.
2610.14428.COMMENT: No direct match to any criterion. The paper is a case study on agentic retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) for customer support workflows, focusing on practical deployment rather than methodological improvements to instruction-following or RLHF.

2610.17391.title: Learning to Play: Reinforcement Learning and Games
2610.17391.abstract: arXiv:2610.17391v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Amazing breakthroughs in reinforcement learning have taken place. Computers teach themselves to play Chess and Go and beat world champions. There is talk about expanding application areas towards general artificial intelligence (AI). The breakthroughs in Backgammon, Checkers, Chess, Atari, Go, Poker, and StarCraft have shown that we can build machines that exhibit intelligent game playing of the highest level. These successes have been widely publicized in the media, and inspire AI entrepreneurs and scientists alike. Reinforcement learning in games has become a mainstream AI research topic. It is a broad topic, and the successes build on a range of diverse techniques, from exact planning algorithms, to adaptive sampling, deep function approximation, and ingenious self-play methods. Perhaps because of the breadth of these technologies, or because of the recency of the breakthroughs, there are few books that explain these methods in depth. This book covers all methods in one comprehensive volume, explaining the latest research, bringing you as close as possible to working implementations, with many references to the original research papers. The programming examples in this book are in Python, the language in which most current reinforcement learning research is conducted. We help you to get started with machine learning frameworks such as Gym, TensorFlow, and Keras, and provide exercises to help understand how AI is learning to play.
2610.17391.COMMENT: No direct match to any specific criterion. The paper is a broad survey/book on reinforcement learning and games, not focused on RLHF or instruction-following fine-tuning methods or other specific criteria.
